source_text: ηβον εἶναι γένος, καὶ χαλινῶν τῶν εἰς ἐγκράτειαν οὐ λίαν ἀνέχεται. Ἀλλ' ἦν ἀκλόνητος ὁ θεσπέσιος Ἰωσὴφ, οὐ τὸ τῆς νεότητος ἀνειμένον ἀπαιδαγώγητον ἔχων, οὐ δεδιὼς ὅτι ξένος ἦν καὶ οἰκέτης. Ἐκβεβίαστο γὰρ εἰς ἄμφω παρὰ τῶν ἀδελφῶν τοῖς Ἰσμαηλίταις καταπωλούμενος. Ἐπεὶ δὲ κρείττων ἦν ἡδονῆς τε ἅμα τῆς μυσαρωτάτης, καὶ τῶν εἰς ἀσέλγειαν κινημάτων, συκοφαντεῖ τὸ γύναιον, καὶ ἀντίστροφον τῷ νέῳ ποιεῖται τὴν γραφήν. Τὸν δὲ, οὐκ εἴκοντα τοῖς αὐτῆς αἰτήμασιν, ὑβριστὴν ἀπεκάλει. Καὶ δεσμώτης μὲν ἐντεῦθεν ὁ νεανίας ἦν· θείᾳ γε μὴν χάριτι διεσώζετο, καὶ μισθὸν ἐγκρατείας ἀποκεκέρδηκεν εὐθὺς, τὸ ἁπάσης κατάρξαι τῆς Αἰγυπτίων χώρας. Οὐκοῦν κἂν εἰ ἔχοι τὸ χρῆμα πόνους, κἂν ἱδρῶτες προκέοιντο βαρεῖς τῶν εἰς ἐγκράτειαν αὐχημάτων, οὐ πολὺς ὁ λόγος, τῷ γε ὅλως φιλοθεεῖν ᾑρημένῳ· ἕξει γὰρ, ἕξει καὶ ἰσοπαλῆ τὸν ἔπαινον, καὶ ἰσοῤῥόπους τὰς ἀμοιβάς. Τοιγάρτοι καὶ ὁ θεσπέσιος Δαβὶδ, ταῖς ἐπὶ τοῦτο τληπαθείαις ἀποθαυμάζει λέγων, τὸν ἀξιεπαινετώτατον νεανίαν, «Εἰς δοῦλον ἐπράθη Ἰωσὴφ, ἐταπείνωσαν ἐν πέδαις τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ, σίδηρον διῆλθεν ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ.» Σίδηρον, οἶμαι, λέγων, τὴν σκληρὰν καὶ ἄθραυστον τῶν ἱδρώτων προσβολὴν, δι' ὧν ἂν γένοιτο καταστέλλειν ἁμαρτίας καὶ ῥύπου παντὸς ἀποφοιτᾷν, τῆς γε μὴν ἁγίας καὶ καθαρωτάτης ἐφικέσθαι ζωῆς, φημὶ δὴ τῆς εὐαγγελικῆς τε καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ, δι' οὗ καὶ μεθ' οὗ τῷ Πατρὶ δόξα, σὺν ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.
pass_a_gloss: [Cyril continuing]...the adolescent kind... does not much endure the bridles toward self-control. But the wondrous Joseph was unshakable, not having the relaxed (pf. ptc), untutored [manner] of youth, not fearing that he was a stranger and a household servant. For he had been forced into both by his brothers, being sold off to the Ishmaelites. And since he was stronger than both the most abominable pleasure and the movements toward licentiousness, the little woman slanders and makes the indictment reversed against the young man. And him, not yielding to her requests, she called an outrager. And from this the youth was a prisoner; yet by divine grace he was kept safe, and he gained at once as wage of self-control to rule over the whole land of the Egyptians. Therefore even if the matter should have labors, even if heavy sweats should lie before the boasts toward self-control, not great is the account for the one who has chosen to love God wholly; for he will have, he will have both equally matched praise and equally balanced rewards. Wherefore the wondrous David also, at the endurances of suffering for this, greatly admires the most praiseworthy young man, saying 'Joseph was sold for a slave; they humbled his feet in fetters; his soul passed through iron.' By iron, I think, meaning the hard and unbreakable assault of the sweats, through which it may be possible to restrain sin and to depart from all filth, and indeed to attain the holy and most pure life, I mean the evangelical one and that in Christ, through whom and with whom to the Father be glory, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of the ages. Amen.
pass_b_english: Cyril: But the wondrous Joseph was unshaken. He did not have the loose, undisciplined ways of youth, nor was he afraid because he was a foreigner and a household slave; for he had been forced into both by his brothers when they sold him to the Ishmaelites (Genesis 37:28). And since he was stronger alike than that most loathsome pleasure and than the stirrings toward lewdness, the wretched woman slandered him and turned the charge round against the young man (Genesis 39:17–19). He would not yield to her demands, and she branded him an assailant. From then on the young man was a prisoner (Genesis 39:20); yet by divine grace he was kept safe, and at once he won, as the wage of his self-control, rule over the whole land of the Egyptians (Genesis 41:41). So even if this course brings labors, even if heavy sweat lies before the glories of self-control, it counts for little with one who has chosen to love God wholly. For he will have, yes, he will have praise to match it and rewards of equal weight. That is why the inspired David too marvels at the most praiseworthy young man for what he suffered in this cause, saying, ‘Joseph was sold as a slave; they humbled his feet in fetters; his soul passed through iron’ (Psalm 105:17–18). By iron, I think, he means the hard and unbreakable onset of such sweat, through which one may hold sin in check and depart from all filth, and indeed attain the holy and most pure life, I mean the life of the Gospel, the life in Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De adoratione Book 14 exists to compare. Translated fresh from the Migne PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the withheld earlier English was not used as a base.

apparatus.note: Migne PG 68 print; the column break may cut a sentence or a word.

Section 32 continues Cyril's speech from section 31 with no new speaker turn; it opens with 'Cyril:' because every section in this book names its speaker; the half-word at the start (ηβον) and its clause are rendered at the end of section 31. Book 14 ends here with the doxology. LXX renumbering: Cyril quotes LXX Psalm 104:17b-18 (Εἰς δοῦλον ἐπράθη Ἰωσήφ ... σίδηρον διῆλθεν ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ), cited as English Psalm 105:17-18; 'his soul passed through iron' follows the LXX (the Hebrew reads differently), and Cyril's comment depends on that wording. The slander ('turned the charge round') is cited to Genesis 39:17-19, where she repeats her accusation to her husband; ὑβριστής (one who commits outrage) rendered 'assailant'. Rule over Egypt cited to Genesis 41:41 ('I have set you over all the land of Egypt'); 41:43 says the same. The historic presents συκοφαντεῖ ... ποιεῖται are rendered in the past tense for English narrative flow. ἱδρῶτες ('sweats') kept as 'sweat' in both places because Cyril's gloss on 'iron' points back to it (τῶν ἱδρώτων); 'sweat before glory' echoes a classical commonplace (Hesiod, Works and Days 289), not Scripture, so no citation. τῶν εἰς ἐγκράτειαν αὐχημάτων ('the boasts toward self-control') rendered 'before one can glory in self-control'. τληπάθεια rendered 'what he suffered'.
removed added causal 'so' before 'she branded him an assailant' (participle carries no cause)
checked Genesis 37:28, 39:17-19, 39:20, 41:41 and LXX Psalm 104:17b-18 = English Psalm 105:17-18 ('his soul passed through iron' is LXX wording)
